ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Endocrinology Referral — Jane Austen — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: New patient visit for about three months of tiredness, weight loss, darkening skin, nausea and back ache, with blood tests and urgent endocrinology referral

text.paragraph: Suspected primary adrenal insufficiency in a 40-year-old novelist with about three months of tiredness, weight loss, darkening skin, nausea and back ache, a postural fall in blood pressure, low sodium, high potassium and raised eosinophils. Please confirm or exclude the diagnosis, start replacement if confirmed, and plan the search for the cause. [S]
Urgency: Urgent, within three days; she is stable today and has been told to go to the emergency department at once for vomiting, fainting, confusion or severe abdominal pain. [S]

list.item: Does she have primary adrenal insufficiency, and which tests confirm it?
Should replacement start at once, and at what doses of hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone?
How should the cause be established, and when are adrenal imaging and tuberculosis testing needed?
Should lymphoma be kept in the differential, given her weight loss and evening feverishness, and how should it be excluded?
What sick-day rules, emergency supplies and follow-up do you advise, including screening for associated autoimmune disease?

text.paragraph: Since the winter she has become steadily more tired, cutting her writing from full mornings to an hour or two, with poor appetite, morning nausea and occasional vomiting, a loss of 5 kg from her usual 57 kg, a dull low back ache by evening, salt craving, and lightheadedness on standing. She has noticed her face and hands darkening. She feels feverish on some evenings but has no drenching night sweats, cough, or lumps that she has noticed. She was very ill with a fever as a young child; no other serious illness. No medicines, including no corticosteroids by any route, and no known allergy. Today: weight 52.0 kg (BMI 18.0), blood pressure 98/62 seated with a postural fall, pulse 92, temperature 37.4 °C; bronze pigmentation of the face, hands, palmar creases and gums; no lymph nodes or enlarged spleen. Results today: sodium 131, potassium 5.4, chloride 99, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, urea nitrogen 23 and creatinine 0.94 mg/dL, eGFR 79, glucose 72 mg/dL, calcium 10.1 mg/dL; hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL with MCV 89 fL, white cells 5.8 with eosinophils 0.74 x10^3/uL, platelets 262; TSH 3.6 mIU/L, free T4 1.1 ng/dL; ferritin 64 ng/mL, vitamin B12 486 pg/mL, folate 11.2 ng/mL. PHQ-9 6, carried by tiredness, appetite and sleep. She has brought written notes on her symptoms since the winter and would like them read [S]

list.item: She has felt worn out for months and is losing weight, and her face and hands have darkened; she wants to know what is wrong. [S]
She wants enough energy to finish the novel she is revising and to walk out again. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Jane Austen was born at the Rectory in Steventon, a village in north-east Hampshire, on 16 December 1775, the seventh child and second daughter of the rector, the Revd George Austen, and his wife Cassandra (née Leigh). [D]

Steventon Rectory was her home for the first 25 years of her life; after some years in Bath and Southampton she moved in 1809 with her mother and sister to a cottage at Chawton, on one of her brother Edward's Hampshire estates, where she revised her early novels and wrote Mansfield Park, Emma and Persuasion. [D]
Her only sister, Cassandra, like Jane herself, never married. [D]
In 1783, as a young child at school in Southampton with her sister, she caught a putrid fever and was very ill and nearly died. [D]
The chronology in the 1913 family biography dates the first break in her health to about March 1816. [D]
Her father died on 21 January 1805 after an illness of only forty-eight hours. [D]

text.paragraph: 14 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
No medications started by this date.

list.item: Novelist; writes most mornings at a small table in the family sitting room, and revises a novel under contract; has had four novels published [S]
Never married; no children; lives with her mother and her older sister in a village cottage; walks to the nearby market town for errands [S]
Tobacco: never. Alcohol: a glass of wine with dinner once or twice a week. No drug use [S]
Activity: walked several miles most days until this winter; now walks less because of tiredness [S]
Keeps a detailed written account of her symptoms in her letters and a notebook, and brings notes to visits; prefers to make light of illness in company [S]
Supports: a close bond with her sister, many nieces and nephews who write often, and work she finds absorbing [S]

list.item: About three months of increasing tiredness, loss of 5 kg, darkening of the skin, nausea with bouts of vomiting, low back ache, salt craving and lightheadedness on standing, with low sodium, high potassium and raised eosinophils; adrenal insufficiency suspected and urgent endocrinology testing booked: active, confirmed [S]
Mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL) with normal ferritin, vitamin B12 and folate: active, confirmed [S]

Initial evaluation of tiredness, weight loss, darkening skin, low sodium and high potassium: blood count, metabolic panel, thyroid tests, ferritin, vitamin B12 and folate at the first visit; urgent 8 am cortisol and ACTH with a cosyntropin stimulation test within days; until then, salt freely, and go to the emergency department at once for vomiting, fainting, confusion or severe abdominal pain. Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (2016); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, anemia monograph (2026) [S]

Anemia: ferritin, vitamin B12 and folate at intake; repeat the blood count on treatment and look further only if it does not recover. Guideline: CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, anemia monograph (2026) [S]
Referral to endocrinology, Lucien Varga-Whitlock, MD, ordered 1816-03-16 [S]
